theme: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me, the suffering king
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 22:1-21. This is the psalm Jesus quoted from the cross. Read it in its own setting first, as David’s cry. Then read it again with Good Friday in mind.
settingTheScene: Psalm 22 is a psalm of David, titled “According to The Doe of the Dawn.” We do not know the event that prompted it, and it uses language that goes beyond anything recorded in David’s life. It begins in the deepest abandonment and ends in universal praise. Placed after the covenant of 2 Samuel 7, it shows that the promised King will suffer before he reigns. Today’s reading covers the first twenty-one verses, the lament.
observation: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me?” (v. 1).
“O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest” (v. 2).
“But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people” (v. 6).
“All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads” (v. 7).
“He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him!” (v. 8).
“I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint; my heart is like wax” (v. 14).
“For dogs encompass me; a company of evildoers encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet” (v. 16).
“They divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots” (v. 18).
interpretation:
Read as David’s own cry, this psalm describes the experience of feeling abandoned by God while surrounded by enemies. The opening words are shocking. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” David does not say, “Why have you stopped helping?” He says, “You have forsaken me.” The Bible permits us to pray the language of felt abandonment. It does not hide it.

But even in the question, there is faith. He still says “My God.” The psalm contains a long review of what God has done in the past: “In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them.” David cannot square the past with the present. This tension is the heart of a lament. He does not resolve it with a quick answer. He keeps praying.

The imagery is graphic. “A worm and not a man.” Mockers wag their heads. “I am poured out like water.” Bones out of joint. A tongue stuck to the jaws. A pack of dogs. Hands and feet pierced. Garments divided by lot. David describes his suffering in terms that go far beyond what history records of him. These details were fulfilled in the death of Jesus, almost word for word.

At the end of the section the tone shifts. Verses 19 to 21 are a cry for help: “But you, O LORD, do not be far off! O you my help, come quickly to my aid!” He finishes with “You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen.” Even in the pit, he knows who to call.

This psalm shows us that the suffering of the righteous is not a sign of God’s absence. It is part of the pattern of how God’s anointed enters into glory. It prepares us for the cross.
connection: Jesus cried the first line of this psalm from the cross (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34). The mockery of verses 7 and 8 is repeated by the passersby and chief priests (Matthew 27:39-43). The dividing of garments is quoted in John 19:24. The thirst of verse 15 is in John 19:28. The piercing of hands and feet is seen in the crucifixion itself. Jesus entered the darkness of abandonment so that we would never be truly forsaken (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 13:5).
application:
If you are in a season of feeling far from God, pray this psalm. Do not hide.

Read the crucifixion account in John 19 alongside this psalm, and notice the details.

Thank Jesus that he was forsaken so you would not be.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being forsaken so that you would not be.
Tell God where you feel far from him.
Praise him that he is near and has not hidden his face.
